# Open Instructional Systems — Full Specification

Version: 0.1.0-alpha
Generated: 2026-05-01T21:18:31.741Z

---

## What is OIS?

Open Instructional Systems (OIS) is a pedagogical design system — a set of tokens, patterns, and themes that describe instructional intent in learning materials. It gives instructors, platforms, and AI agents a shared vocabulary for the "how" of teaching, not just the "what."

---

## Tokens

### accessibility.mode
Category: accessibility
Type: enum
Definition: The primary accessibility design orientation of the learning experience.
Default: standard
Values:
    standard: Standard accessibility compliance (WCAG 2.1 AA).
    low-bandwidth: Designed to function in limited connectivity environments.
    screen-reader-first: Content is primarily designed for screen reader accessibility.
    multimodal: Content is available in multiple sensory modalities.
    flexible-deadline: Time-based constraints are minimized or eliminated.
    universal-design: Full Universal Design for Learning principles applied.

### accessibility.mediaAlternatives
Category: accessibility
Type: enum-multi
Definition: The accessible alternatives provided for media-based content.
Values:
    captions: Synchronized text captions for video or audio content.
    transcript: Full text transcript of audio or video content.
    alt-text: Text descriptions of images and visual content.
    printable: Print-ready versions of all materials.
    audio-description: Audio narration of visual information for video content.
    downloadable-assets: All assets available for offline download.

### agency.mode
Category: agency
Type: enum
Definition: The degree of learner choice and self-direction in the learning experience.
Default: bounded-choice
Values:
    fixed-path: The learner follows a predetermined sequence with no choices.
    bounded-choice: The learner chooses within defined options provided by the instructor.
    open-choice: The learner defines their own direction within the domain.
    self-directed: The learner sets goals, selects methods, and evaluates their own progress.

### agency.choicePoint
Category: agency
Type: enum-multi
Definition: The dimension(s) where learner choice is exercised.
Values:
    topic: Learner chooses what to study or investigate.
    tool: Learner chooses which tools or technologies to use.
    medium: Learner chooses the output format or medium.
    sequence: Learner chooses the order of activities.
    partner: Learner chooses collaborators.
    deliverable: Learner chooses the form of the final product.
    audience: Learner chooses who their work is for.

### aiUse.policy
Category: aiUse
Type: enum
Definition: The policy governing learner use of AI tools in this activity.
Default: not-specified
Values:
    prohibited: AI tools are not permitted in this activity.
    not-specified: No AI use policy has been defined. Not recommended for new content.
    instructor-specified: The instructor will specify AI use rules outside this content block.
    permitted-undisclosed: AI use is permitted but disclosure is not required. Use sparingly.
    assisted-disclosed: AI assistance is permitted and must be disclosed.
    collaborative-disclosed: AI is used as a collaborative partner; disclosure and reflection required.
    experimental: Learners are explicitly using AI as the subject of investigation.
AI Guidance: Never set to anything other than prohibited without also setting aiUse.disclosureRequired to true.

### aiUse.allowedFunctions
Category: aiUse
Type: enum-multi
Definition: The specific AI functions permitted in this activity.
Values:
    brainstorming: AI may be used to brainstorm and generate initial ideas.
    outlining: AI may be used to create outlines and structural plans.
    debugging: AI may be used to debug code or identify logical errors.
    critique: AI may be used to critique drafts or designs.
    feedback: AI may be used to provide feedback on drafts or work-in-progress.
    reference-generation: AI may be used to generate or locate references and sources.
    image-generation: AI may be used to generate images.
    code-generation: AI may be used to generate code.
    final-artifact-generation: AI may be used to generate the final submission artifact.
AI Guidance: Be specific. List only permitted functions. Never leave unspecified when aiUse.policy is not prohibited.

### aiUse.disclosureRequired
Category: aiUse
Type: boolean
Definition: Whether learners must disclose their AI use in this activity.
Default: false

### aiUse.reflectionRequired
Category: aiUse
Type: boolean
Definition: Whether learners must submit a reflection on their AI use.
Default: false

### assessment.evidence
Category: assessment
Type: enum
Definition: The primary form of evidence collected to demonstrate learning.
Default: artifact
Values:
    quiz: A knowledge check or test with predetermined correct answers.
    artifact: A tangible product created by the learner.
    performance: A live or recorded demonstration of skill.
    portfolio: A curated collection of work over time.
    reflection: Written or recorded personal reflection on learning.
    critique-notes: Documentation produced during a critique or review session.
    process-documentation: Evidence of the learning process itself (sketches, drafts, logs).
    presentation: A structured presentation to an audience.
    artifact-plus-reflection: A finished product accompanied by a required reflection.

### assessment.mode
Category: assessment
Type: enum
Definition: The purpose or function of the assessment in the learning arc.
Default: formative
Values:
    formative: Assessment used to guide ongoing learning; low-stakes.
    summative: Assessment of learning at the end of a unit; higher-stakes.
    diagnostic: Assessment used to identify prior knowledge or gaps before instruction.
    ipsative: Assessment comparing learner to their own prior performance.
    mastery: Assessment that must be passed at a threshold before advancement.
    critique-based: Assessment conducted through structured group critique.

### collaboration.structure
Category: collaboration
Type: enum
Definition: How learners are organized for collaborative work.
Default: individual
Values:
    individual: Each learner works alone.
    pair: Learners work in pairs.
    small-group: Learners work in groups of 3-6.
    peer-review: Learners review each other's work in a structured exchange.
    studio-critique: Work is shared and critiqued in a group critique format.
    community-partner: Collaboration involves a real external community partner.

### collaboration.roleClarity
Category: collaboration
Type: enum
Definition: How explicitly roles are defined within collaborative work.
Default: none
Values:
    none: No role definitions given.
    informal: Roles emerge organically without formal assignment.
    assigned-roles: Specific roles are assigned by the instructor.
    rotating-roles: Roles rotate across activities or sessions.

### feedback.mode
Category: feedback
Type: enum
Definition: Who provides feedback on learner work.
Default: instructor
Values:
    none: No feedback is given.
    self: Learner evaluates their own work.
    peer: Another learner provides feedback.
    instructor: The instructor provides feedback.
    automated: Feedback is system-generated.
    community: Feedback comes from a community partner or external audience.
    peer-plus-instructor: Both peer and instructor feedback are provided.
    mixed: Multiple feedback sources are used.

### feedback.timing
Category: feedback
Type: enum
Definition: When feedback is provided relative to the submission or activity.
Default: after-submission
Values:
    before-submission: Feedback is given before the learner finalizes work (e.g., draft review).
    during-process: Feedback is given during the activity (e.g., coaching, in-process check-ins).
    after-submission: Feedback is given after the learner submits.
    iterative: Multiple rounds of feedback are built into the design.
    on-demand: Learner requests feedback when ready.

### localization.level
Category: localization
Type: enum
Definition: The depth of localization applied to the learning materials.
Default: none
Values:
    none: No localization. Original language and examples only.
    language-only: Text is translated but examples remain from the original cultural context.
    examples-localized: Both language and examples are adapted to the target cultural context.
    culturally-adapted: Deeper cultural adaptation including values, norms, and local context.
    community-co-designed: Materials were co-designed with members of the target community.

### bandwidth.assumption
Category: localization
Type: enum
Definition: The assumed internet connectivity level for learners.
Default: medium
Values:
    low: Assumes limited or intermittent connectivity (< 1 Mbps).
    medium: Assumes moderate broadband connectivity.
    high: Assumes reliable high-speed internet.
    offline-capable: All materials must function without internet access.

### reflection.required
Category: reflection
Type: boolean
Definition: Whether structured reflection is a required component of the learning activity.
Default: false

### reflection.focus
Category: reflection
Type: enum-multi
Definition: The subject or lens of the required reflection.
Values:
    process: Reflecting on how the learner approached the task.
    concept-transfer: Reflecting on how concepts apply to other contexts.
    creative-choice: Reflecting on aesthetic or design decisions made.
    ethical-use: Reflecting on ethical dimensions, especially AI use or community impact.
    collaboration: Reflecting on how the group worked together.
    failure-analysis: Reflecting on what didn't work and why.
    metacognition: Reflecting on one's own learning and thinking strategies.

### revision.required
Category: revision
Type: boolean
Definition: Whether learners are required to revise their work after feedback.
Default: false

### revision.mode
Category: revision
Type: enum
Definition: The structure of the revision requirement.
Values:
    optional: Revision is available but not required.
    required-once: One revision cycle is required.
    required-until-proficient: The learner must revise until meeting the proficiency threshold.
    iterative-cycle: Multiple structured revision cycles are built into the design.

### scaffolding.level
Category: scaffolding
Type: enum
Definition: The degree of instructional support provided to the learner.
Default: medium
Values:
    none: No scaffolding. Learner must self-direct entirely. (use when: Expert learners only.)
    low: Minimal prompts or guiding questions only. (use when: Intermediate to advanced learners with prior domain knowledge.)
    medium: Some structure, examples, or guiding questions provided. (use when: Mixed experience levels; most adult learners.)
    high: Worked examples, templates, checklists, and step-by-step guidance. (use when: Novice or early-stage learners; high-stakes tasks.)
    adaptive: Scaffolding adjusts dynamically based on learner progress. (use when: Platforms with adaptive learning capabilities.)
AI Guidance: Match scaffolding level to learner experience. Beginners need high; advanced learners benefit from low to build agency.

### scaffolding.type
Category: scaffolding
Type: enum
Definition: The primary modality of instructional support provided.
Values:
    worked-example: A solved problem or completed example provided for reference.
    checklist: A list of steps or criteria the learner can check off.
    template: A partially completed structure for the learner to fill in.
    guided-steps: A sequential set of instructions that walk the learner through the task.
    exemplar: A high-quality example of a finished product for comparison.
    coaching: Ongoing feedback from an instructor or peer throughout the process.
    none: No scaffolding type. Used with scaffolding.level none.
AI Guidance: Use in combination with scaffolding.level. If scaffolding.level is high, specify the scaffolding.type so AI agents can generate the right support materials.


---

## Patterns

### artifact-analysis-reflection
Learners closely analyze an existing artifact, then reflect on its significance, method, and meaning.
Problem: How do you develop close reading and critical analysis skills through artifact engagement?
Sequence:
  1. Artifact Encounter
     Learner: Encounter the artifact without interpretive guidance. Note your initial reactions, observations, and questions.
     Instructor: Select artifact and withhold context. Ask for unguided first impressions before providing background.
  2. Contextual Analysis
     Learner: Learn the context of the artifact's creation (historical, cultural, authorial). Re-examine the artifact through that context. Note how your reading shifts.
     Instructor: Provide relevant contextual information. Facilitate discussion of how context changes interpretation.
  3. Close Reading
     Learner: Conduct a structured close reading using an analysis framework (semiotics, rhetorical analysis, formal analysis, etc.). Document specific evidence from the artifact.
     Instructor: Provide the analysis framework. Require evidence citation from the artifact itself.
  4. Significance Reflection
     Learner: Write a reflection on what this artifact means, why it matters, and what you understand differently having studied it.
     Instructor: Assess both the analytical rigor of the close reading and the depth of the significance reflection.
AI Guidance: When generating close reading prompts, specify the analysis framework explicitly. Do not ask for "what do you think?" — ask for evidence-anchored claims. The significance reflection should push beyond description to interpretation and personal meaning-making.

### case-stakeholder-analysis-response-design
Learners examine a complex case, analyze the perspectives of affected stakeholders, and design a justified response.
Problem: How do you develop ethical reasoning and policy thinking in courses where there are no simple right answers?
Sequence:
  1. Case Presentation
     Learner: Read, watch, or listen to a case study representing a complex real-world problem. Take notes on the key facts, actors, and tensions.
     Instructor: Present or curate the case. Provide sufficient context for learners to understand complexity. Do not resolve tensions prematurely.
  2. Stakeholder Identification
     Learner: Identify all stakeholders affected by the situation. Document each stakeholder's interests, constraints, and likely perspective.
     Instructor: Provide a stakeholder analysis scaffold. Ensure learners include marginalized and non-obvious stakeholders.
  3. Perspective Analysis
     Learner: Write or present a brief perspective statement from each key stakeholder's point of view. Identify tensions between stakeholder interests.
     Instructor: Facilitate perspective-taking discussion. Challenge oversimplifications.
  4. Response Design
     Learner: Design and justify a response to the case that acknowledges stakeholder interests and states trade-offs explicitly.
     Instructor: Assess response on clarity of reasoning, acknowledgment of complexity, and quality of justification — not on position taken.
AI Guidance: When generating content for this pattern, do not resolve the case tensions. Provide a rich, ambiguous case. Scaffold the stakeholder analysis before the response design phase. The assessment should not privilege any single political or ethical stance.

### community-contextualized-design-brief
Learners design a real artifact for a real community partner, contextualizing all production decisions in community needs.
Problem: How do you create authentic learning experiences that generate real value for real people outside the classroom?
Sequence:
  1. Community Partner Introduction
     Learner: Meet or learn about the community partner. Document the partner's context, needs, constraints, and goals. Resist proposing solutions at this stage.
     Instructor: Arrange community partner engagement. Scaffold active listening. Suppress the "design instinct" to jump to solutions.
  2. Needs Analysis
     Learner: Analyze the partner's needs through the lens of this course's skills and knowledge. Identify what you can realistically offer and what is beyond scope.
     Instructor: Guide learners to calibrate ambition to capacity. Ensure learners are not over-promising.
  3. Design and Iteration
     Learner: Design an artifact addressing a specific documented need. Share drafts or prototypes with the partner for feedback. Revise in response to partner input.
     Instructor: Facilitate partner feedback sessions. Ensure learners are listening, not defending.
  4. Delivery and Reflection
     Learner: Deliver the final artifact to the partner. Reflect on the design process, the community context, your role, and what you would do differently.
     Instructor: Assess both artifact quality and quality of reflection on community engagement.
AI Guidance: When generating design briefs for this pattern, center the community partner's actual stated needs. Do not invent a community or fabricate needs. If generating a simulated partner, make the simulation explicit. Reflection should engage with power dynamics and positionality, not just process description.

### constraint-based-project-sprint
Learners produce an artifact under explicit constraints, emphasizing rapid iteration and decisive creative choices.
Problem: How do you develop creative confidence and decision-making speed in learners who over-plan and under-produce?
Sequence:
  1. Brief and Constraints
     Learner: Receive the project brief and explicit constraints (time limit, material restrictions, required elements, excluded approaches). Ask clarifying questions.
     Instructor: State constraints clearly and explain their purpose. Constraints should be meaningful, not arbitrary.
  2. Rapid Ideation
     Learner: Generate multiple divergent ideas (3–5 minimum) before committing to any. Use sketches, outlines, or quick prototypes.
     Instructor: Facilitate timed ideation. Encourage quantity over quality at this phase.
  3. Committed Production
     Learner: Select one direction and produce a complete artifact within the allotted time. Prioritize completion over perfection.
     Instructor: Set and hold firm time limits. Resist requests for extensions — deadline pressure is pedagogically intentional.
  4. Process Debrief
     Learner: Reflect on the constraints: which helped, which hurt, what decisions you would change, and what the constraint revealed about your process.
     Instructor: Facilitate whole-class debrief. Focus on creative decision-making under pressure.
AI Guidance: Generate constraints that are specific and meaningful. Avoid constraints that merely restrict scope without shaping creative decisions. The debrief prompt should ask about constraint experience, not just artifact quality.

### demo-guided-practice-independent-production
Instructor demonstrates a skill or technique, learners practice with support, then apply independently.
Problem: How do you teach procedural or technical skills to novices who need to see before they do?
Sequence:
  1. Demonstration
     Learner: Observe the instructor demonstration. Take notes on each step and note points of difficulty or confusion.
     Instructor: Demonstrate the target skill step-by-step while narrating decisions and common mistakes. Use think-aloud protocol.
  2. Guided Practice
     Learner: Attempt the skill with a provided scaffold (template, checklist, guided worksheet, or worked example). Ask questions as needed.
     Instructor: Circulate or monitor asynchronous submissions. Provide targeted feedback. Allow multiple attempts on the guided exercise.
  3. Formative Check
     Learner: Receive instructor or peer feedback on guided practice. Identify gaps and revise before independent work.
     Instructor: Provide written or verbal feedback. Identify patterns across class and address common errors.
  4. Independent Production
     Learner: Apply the skill without scaffolding to a new but analogous task. Produce the final artifact.
     Instructor: Assess independently produced work against criteria. Offer revision opportunity if appropriate.
AI Guidance: When generating content for this pattern, produce a demonstration walkthrough first, then a scaffolded exercise version, then an independent exercise version. Each version should clearly state its scaffolding level.

### mastery-checkpoint-pathway
Learners progress through skill levels, demonstrating mastery at each checkpoint before advancing.
Problem: How do you ensure all learners reach genuine proficiency before moving to the next skill level?
Sequence:
  1. Skill Introduction
     Learner: Review the learning objective and mastery criteria for this checkpoint. Understand what proficiency looks like before beginning.
     Instructor: Present the skill in context. Make the mastery criteria explicit. Connect to prior skills.
  2. Scaffolded Practice
     Learner: Work through scaffolded practice exercises from guided to independent. Identify where errors occur and use them as learning signals.
     Instructor: Provide worked examples, then remove scaffolding gradually. Allow unlimited low-stakes attempts.
  3. Checkpoint Attempt
     Learner: Attempt the mastery checkpoint. This is a genuine demonstration, not a practice exercise.
     Instructor: Evaluate against explicit mastery criteria. Pass or not-yet. If not-yet, provide specific feedback on gaps.
  4. Remediation and Re-attempt (if needed)
     Learner: If not-yet, address specific gaps identified in feedback. Attempt additional practice. Re-attempt the checkpoint.
     Instructor: Facilitate targeted remediation. Ensure the re-attempt tests the same objective with a parallel (not identical) task.
AI Guidance: When generating checkpoint assessments, ensure the mastery criteria are specific and observable. Scaffolded practice and checkpoint should test the same skill with different tasks. Mastery is binary (pass/not-yet) — not a gradient.

### observe-analyze-create-critique-revise
A studio-based cycle where learners study exemplars, analyze structure, make original work, receive critique, and revise.
Problem: How do you design a learning experience where making, feedback, and revision are the core of learning — not supplemental?
Sequence:
  1. Observe
     Learner: Study 2-3 exemplars of finished work in the target form.
     Instructor: Curate exemplars that represent the range of quality and approach. Prompt observation with guiding questions.
  2. Analyze
     Learner: Identify patterns, techniques, decisions, and what makes each exemplar effective or not.
     Instructor: Facilitate structured analysis using a common vocabulary or rubric.
  3. Create
     Learner: Produce original work in response to the brief.
     Instructor: Circulate, offer coaching feedback during process.
  4. Critique
     Learner: Present work to peers; receive structured feedback using established criteria.
     Instructor: Facilitate critique. Model feedback language. Keep critique focused on work, not person.
  5. Revise
     Learner: Revise work based on critique. Document what changed and why.
     Instructor: Review revision with attention to responsiveness to feedback.
AI Guidance: When generating materials for this pattern, produce both a student-facing brief (phases 1-5 as instructions) and a studio critique guide for the instructor. Ensure the exemplars section specifies what to observe. Do not skip the revision phase.

### peer-review-studio-cycle
Learners produce a draft, give and receive structured peer critique, then revise based on feedback.
Problem: How do you build a culture of critical feedback and iterative improvement in a writing or production course?
Sequence:
  1. Draft Production
     Learner: Produce a complete first draft or prototype. Label it clearly as a draft and identify two or three areas you want feedback on.
     Instructor: Set clear draft submission requirements. Clarify what "complete draft" means — not a rough outline.
  2. Peer Critique
     Learner: Review an assigned peer's draft using a structured critique guide. Provide specific, evidence-based feedback. Avoid vague praise or criticism.
     Instructor: Provide a critique guide with explicit criteria. Facilitate brief norms discussion before critique begins.
  3. Feedback Reception
     Learner: Read all peer feedback. Identify patterns. Ask clarifying questions if needed. Do not defend your draft at this stage.
     Instructor: Facilitate structured feedback reception (optional). Ensure learners are reading, not dismissing, peer feedback.
  4. Revision
     Learner: Revise the artifact in response to feedback. Document which feedback you acted on and why, and which you chose not to use and why.
     Instructor: Review revision documentation alongside final artifact. Assess the quality of revision reasoning, not just the artifact.
AI Guidance: When generating critique guides, provide specific criteria anchored to the learning objectives — not generic writing advice. The revision memo is as important as the artifact. Assess reasoning, not just outcomes.

### prompt-ai-experiment-evaluate-disclose
Learners craft a prompt, run an AI experiment, critically evaluate the output, and disclose their process.
Problem: How do you teach critical AI use when learners lack frameworks for evaluating AI output?
Sequence:
  1. Prompt Design
     Learner: Design and document a prompt intended to produce a specified outcome. Consider specificity, context, and constraints.
     Instructor: Provide exemplar prompts and non-examples. Facilitate discussion of what makes a prompt effective.
  2. AI Experiment
     Learner: Run the prompt through one or more AI tools. Document the outputs without editing them.
     Instructor: Ensure access to appropriate tools. Clarify ethical and policy constraints on tool use.
  3. Evaluate Output
     Learner: Evaluate the AI output against explicit criteria: accuracy, bias, gaps, usefulness, limitations. Revise the prompt if needed and document iterations.
     Instructor: Provide an evaluation rubric. Facilitate whole-class discussion of common AI failure modes.
  4. Disclose and Reflect
     Learner: Complete an AI Use Disclosure (AIUL) documenting which tools were used, what functions they served, and what the learner contributed.
     Instructor: Review disclosures for completeness and accuracy.
AI Guidance: When scaffolding this pattern, provide explicit prompt design criteria and evaluation rubrics. Do not allow learners to submit AI output without evaluation. The AIUL declaration is required, not optional.

### reference-study-technical-exercise-creative-application
Learners study exemplars, complete a technical exercise to build foundational skill, then apply it creatively.
Problem: How do you help learners move from technical proficiency to creative ownership?
Sequence:
  1. Reference Study
     Learner: Study a curated set of exemplary works from practitioners in the field. Document specific techniques, decisions, and effects observed.
     Instructor: Curate exemplars representing diverse approaches and contexts. Provide an observation guide.
  2. Technical Exercise
     Learner: Complete a constrained technical exercise that isolates a specific technique observed in the reference study. Focus on precision and control.
     Instructor: Provide step-by-step guidance. Allow multiple attempts. Give targeted technical feedback.
  3. Technique Reflection
     Learner: Reflect on what the technique does and why practitioners might choose to use or avoid it.
     Instructor: Facilitate brief discussion connecting technique to context and intention.
  4. Creative Application
     Learner: Apply the studied technique(s) in an original work of your own design. Make intentional choices and document them.
     Instructor: Assess both the quality of technique and the intentionality of creative decisions.
AI Guidance: When generating exemplars for this pattern, include diverse practitioners and contexts. The creative application phase should specify that learners state their intention — not just submit a product.


---

## Themes

### accessibility-first
A Universal Design for Learning (UDL) style where accessibility is the primary design constraint, not an afterthought.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: medium
  scaffolding.type: multiple-means
  agency.mode: bounded-choice
  feedback.mode: instructor
  feedback.timing: ongoing
  assessment.evidence: portfolio
  assessment.mode: formative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: required-once
  reflection.required: true
  reflection.focus: process
  collaboration.structure: optional
  accessibility.mode: screen-reader-first
  accessibility.mediaAlternatives: alt-text, captions, transcript, downloadable-assets
  localization.level: translated
  bandwidth.assumption: low
  aiUse.policy: assisted-disclosed
Preferred Patterns: demo-guided-practice-independent-production, mastery-checkpoint-pathway
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, every media asset must have an accessible alternative. Assessment evidence must not privilege any single modality. Provide multiple means of representation, expression, and engagement as defined by UDL. Assume all learners may have assistive technology needs.

### ai-literacy
A critical AI use style where AI tools are the subject of investigation — how they work, what they produce, and what they mean.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: medium
  scaffolding.type: guided-questions
  agency.mode: bounded-choice
  feedback.mode: instructor
  feedback.timing: before-submission
  assessment.evidence: artifact-plus-reflection
  assessment.mode: formative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: required-once
  reflection.required: true
  reflection.focus: ethical-use
  collaboration.structure: small-group
  aiUse.policy: experimental
  aiUse.allowedFunctions: brainstorming, outlining, critique, feedback, image-generation, code-generation, final-artifact-generation
  aiUse.disclosureRequired: true
  aiUse.reflectionRequired: true
Preferred Patterns: prompt-ai-experiment-evaluate-disclose, artifact-analysis-reflection
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, AI tools are required, not optional. Learners must document their AI use, evaluate its outputs, and reflect on its implications. Assessment criteria must reward critical evaluation over AI output quality. The AI Use Disclosure (AIUL) is a required deliverable.

### community-engaged
A participatory learning style where real community partners shape the learning brief and receive real deliverables.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: medium
  agency.mode: bounded-choice
  feedback.mode: peer-plus-instructor
  feedback.timing: before-submission
  assessment.evidence: artifact-plus-reflection
  assessment.mode: summative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: multiple-drafts
  reflection.required: true
  reflection.focus: ethical-use
  collaboration.structure: small-group
  collaboration.roleClarity: assigned
  localization.level: co-created
  aiUse.policy: instructor-specified
Preferred Patterns: community-contextualized-design-brief, case-stakeholder-analysis-response-design
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, the community partner's needs must frame the design brief. Learner reflection must address positionality, power, and what the learner's role is relative to the community. Simulated community partners are acceptable but must be explicitly labeled as simulations. Assessment should weigh community benefit and reflective depth, not just artifact quality.

### constructivist-studio
A making-centred pedagogical style where learning happens through creating, critiquing, and revising work.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: medium
  agency.mode: bounded-choice
  feedback.mode: peer-plus-instructor
  feedback.timing: before-submission
  assessment.evidence: artifact-plus-reflection
  assessment.mode: formative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: required-once
  reflection.required: true
  reflection.focus: process
  collaboration.structure: studio-critique
Preferred Patterns: observe-analyze-create-critique-revise, peer-review-studio-cycle, constraint-based-project-sprint
AI Guidance: When generating materials for this theme, foreground making. The project brief should lead with the deliverable and the critique structure, not a reading list. Include a studio critique guide. Reflection should focus on process and creative choices.

### critical-media-analysis
A representation-focused style where learners analyze how media constructs meaning, power, and identity, and respond creatively.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: medium
  scaffolding.type: guided-questions
  agency.mode: bounded-choice
  feedback.mode: instructor
  feedback.timing: before-submission
  assessment.evidence: artifact-plus-reflection
  assessment.mode: formative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: required-once
  reflection.required: true
  reflection.focus: ethical-use
  collaboration.structure: small-group
  aiUse.policy: assisted-disclosed
Preferred Patterns: artifact-analysis-reflection, observe-analyze-create-critique-revise
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, analytical frameworks must be named explicitly (semiotics, representation theory, framing analysis, etc.). Creative response assignments should require learners to make and state intentional choices that engage with the critical analysis. Assessment criteria must reward analytical rigor, not ideological agreement.

### direct-instruction
An explicit, instructor-led teaching style with demonstration, guided practice, and skill verification.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: high
  scaffolding.type: worked-example
  agency.mode: fixed-path
  feedback.mode: instructor
  feedback.timing: after-submission
  assessment.evidence: quiz
  assessment.mode: formative
  revision.required: false
  reflection.required: false
  collaboration.structure: none
  aiUse.policy: prohibited
Preferred Patterns: demo-guided-practice-independent-production, mastery-checkpoint-pathway
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, lead with explicit learning objectives and connect each activity directly to an objective. Worked examples should precede practice. Assessments should test the same skill demonstrated. Keep agency minimal — the learner's job at this stage is to master the defined skill.

### inquiry-based
A question-driven investigative style where learners generate and pursue their own inquiries with instructor support.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: medium
  scaffolding.type: guided-questions
  agency.mode: open-choice
  feedback.mode: instructor
  feedback.timing: ongoing
  assessment.evidence: reflection
  assessment.mode: formative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: multiple-drafts
  reflection.required: true
  reflection.focus: process
  collaboration.structure: small-group
  aiUse.policy: assisted-disclosed
Preferred Patterns: artifact-analysis-reflection, case-stakeholder-analysis-response-design
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, open with a question rather than a statement. Assessment criteria should reward quality of inquiry process as much as quality of conclusions. Resist giving answers too early — sustained productive discomfort is pedagogically valuable here.

### low-bandwidth-global
An OER delivery style designed for under-resourced and offline contexts, prioritizing downloadable assets and low-tech alternatives.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: high
  scaffolding.type: checklist
  agency.mode: fixed-path
  feedback.mode: instructor
  feedback.timing: after-submission
  assessment.evidence: quiz
  assessment.mode: formative
  revision.required: false
  reflection.required: false
  collaboration.structure: none
  accessibility.mode: screen-reader-first
  accessibility.mediaAlternatives: alt-text, transcript, downloadable-assets, print-friendly
  localization.level: culturally-adapted
  bandwidth.assumption: offline-capable
  aiUse.policy: prohibited
Preferred Patterns: demo-guided-practice-independent-production, mastery-checkpoint-pathway
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, every content element must have a low-bandwidth or offline equivalent. No auto-playing media. All assets must be downloadable. Avoid external service dependencies that require internet access at time of use. Assessment must be completable offline or via asynchronous submission.

### mastery-learning
A competency-based style where learners demonstrate proficiency before advancing, with unlimited revision until mastery.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: high
  scaffolding.type: checklist
  agency.mode: fixed-path
  feedback.mode: instructor
  feedback.timing: after-submission
  assessment.evidence: quiz
  assessment.mode: summative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: until-mastery
  reflection.required: false
  collaboration.structure: none
  aiUse.policy: prohibited
Preferred Patterns: mastery-checkpoint-pathway, demo-guided-practice-independent-production
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, make mastery criteria explicit and observable before the activity begins. Assessment is pass/not-yet — never graded on a curve. Re-attempts test the same objective with a parallel (not identical) task. Progress should be gated by demonstrated competency, not time spent.

### project-based-production
An extended authentic project style where learners produce a real artifact for a real or simulated audience through iterative development.
Token Defaults:
  scaffolding.level: low
  agency.mode: bounded-choice
  feedback.mode: peer-plus-instructor
  feedback.timing: before-submission
  assessment.evidence: artifact-plus-reflection
  assessment.mode: summative
  revision.required: true
  revision.mode: multiple-drafts
  reflection.required: true
  reflection.focus: design-decisions
  collaboration.structure: small-group
  collaboration.roleClarity: assigned
  aiUse.policy: collaborative-disclosed
  aiUse.allowedFunctions: brainstorming, outlining, feedback, reference-generation
  aiUse.disclosureRequired: true
Preferred Patterns: observe-analyze-create-critique-revise, peer-review-studio-cycle, community-contextualized-design-brief
AI Guidance: When applying this theme, ensure the project brief specifies a real or simulated audience with real constraints. Multiple feedback cycles before final submission are required, not optional. Assessment should weigh process documentation alongside final product quality.


---

## Validation Rules

### objective-requires-evidence [error]
Learning Objective Requires Assessment Evidence
If: assessment.evidence
Then: assessment.evidence must be present
Message: No assessment evidence type is specified. Every learning activity must define how learning will be evidenced.
Rationale: Without a defined evidence type, there is no basis for evaluating whether learning occurred.

### revision-requires-timely-feedback [error]
Revision Requires Pre-Submission Feedback
If: revision.required in [true]
Then: feedback.timing
Message: revision.required is true but feedback.timing is after-submission. Revision cannot be meaningfully performed without timely feedback.
Rationale: If feedback arrives only after submission, learners cannot revise in the same cycle.

### ai-use-requires-disclosure [error]
AI Use Requires Disclosure
If: aiUse.policy not in [prohibited, not-specified]
Then: aiUse.disclosureRequired must be [true]
Message: aiUse.policy permits AI use but aiUse.disclosureRequired is not set to true.
Rationale: Any non-prohibited AI use must require disclosure for academic integrity.

### ai-collaborative-requires-reflection [error]
Collaborative AI Use Requires Reflection
If: aiUse.policy in [collaborative-disclosed]
Then: reflection.required must be [true]
Message: aiUse.policy is collaborative-disclosed but reflection.required is not true. Collaborative AI use requires reflection.
Rationale: Collaborative AI use involves the highest degree of AI integration. Without reflection, learners cannot develop critical AI literacy.

### low-bandwidth-needs-alternatives [warning]
Low Bandwidth Requires Downloadable Alternatives
If: bandwidth.assumption in [low, offline-capable]
Then: accessibility.mediaAlternatives must include [downloadable-assets]
Message: bandwidth.assumption is low or offline-capable but no downloadable-assets media alternative is specified.
Rationale: Low-bandwidth learners need downloadable assets to access content offline.

---

## Implementation Recipe

1. Fetch /ois-index.json
2. Identify learning goal, learner level, domain, constraints
3. Select theme from themes
4. Select pattern from theme.preferredPatterns
5. Resolve tokens (theme defaults → pattern requirements → local overrides)
6. Run validation rules
7. Generate materials using pattern sequence
8. Output transparency summary
9. Output machine-readable pedagogy block
10. Return to user with validation report
